title: Disasters That Changed the World · Episode 3
chapters: Chernobyl: the night a reactor exploded
Tropical cyclones: anatomy of a monster storm
How people really behave in disasters

units.t: Disasters That Changed the World. Episode three.
In this episode: Chernobyl: the night a reactor exploded, Tropical cyclones: anatomy of a monster storm and How people really behave in disasters.
Part one. Chernobyl: the night a reactor exploded.
In April 1986 a late night safety test went catastrophically wrong in Soviet Ukraine.
The disaster spread radiation across Europe and shook the Soviet Union to its core.
Test, flaw, explosion.
The Chernobyl plant stood in northern Soviet Ukraine, near the new town of Pripyat.
In the early hours of 26 April 1986, a night shift that had not prepared for it ran a test at reactor 4.
They wanted to know whether spinning turbines could keep cooling pumps running briefly if power failed.
Operators reduced the reactor's power and disabled several safety systems.
It became unstable, and they withdrew most of the control rods.
The Soviet RBMK design had dangerous features operators were not fully told about: if cooling water turned to steam, power could rise rather than fall.
When power surged, an operator hit the emergency shutdown, but a flaw in the rods briefly boosted the reaction.
Steam explosions blew apart the reactor, and burning graphite sent radioactive material high into the sky for days.
Firefighters and liquidators.
Firefighters raced to the plant within minutes and fought fires on the roof and around the reactor building.
Few understood how intense the radiation was, and some reportedly picked up chunks of graphite thrown from the core.
Two plant workers died on the night.
In the following weeks and months, around 28 more, mostly firefighters and staff, died from acute radiation sickness, despite treatment in a specialist Moscow hospital.
Helicopters dropped thousands of tonnes of sand, clay, lead and other materials onto the burning reactor to smother it.
Later, miners dug beneath it to install cooling, and huge numbers of workers known as liquidators carried out the cleanup.
Pripyat and the Swedish alarm.
On the day after the explosion, life in Pripyat continued almost as normal.
Children played outside and a wedding went ahead.
About 36 hours after the accident, residents were told to pack for a short evacuation.
Roughly 49,000 people boarded buses believing they would return within days.
They never did.
The zone was widened to about 30 kilometres, and more than 100,000 people were eventually moved.
Soviet authorities said almost nothing.
On 28 April, workers arriving at Sweden's Forsmark plant, more than 1,000 kilometres away, set off radiation alarms.
Swedish experts found nothing wrong at their plant and traced the particles to winds from the Soviet Union.
Under pressure, Soviet state media issued a short statement that evening acknowledging an accident.
Mikhail Gorbachev later suggested Chernobyl exposed the failings of the Soviet system.
Counting the cost.
Radioactive fallout drifted across Belarus, Ukraine and Russia and on to much of Europe, with rain bringing it down unevenly.
Farmers as far away as Wales and Scandinavia faced restrictions on sheep and reindeer for years.
The clearest health effect was a sharp rise in thyroid cancer among people who were children at the time, mainly because radioactive iodine got into milk from cows grazing on contaminated grass.
Thousands of cases were diagnosed, though most patients survived with treatment.
Estimates of eventual cancer deaths vary widely.
A major United Nations-led review in 2005 estimated up to about 4,000 deaths among the most heavily exposed groups, while some studies give much higher figures for Europe.
Many evacuees also suffered serious stress and upheaval, and the economic cost ran into many billions of dollars.
The zone today.
Within months, workers built a concrete shelter, the sarcophagus, over the shattered reactor.
It was rushed and began to deteriorate, so an international project slid an enormous arched steel structure, the New Safe Confinement, over it in 2016.
The last working reactor shut down in 2000.
Pripyat is now a ghost town, its apartment blocks crumbling.
With people gone, the exclusion zone has become an unexpected wildlife refuge for wolves, elk, deer and rare Przewalski's horses, though scientists still debate radiation's effects on animals.
In 2022 Russian troops occupied the site for several weeks during the invasion of Ukraine.
The key idea: A rushed safety test and a flawed reactor design combined to destroy reactor 4 on 26 April 1986.
Part two. Tropical cyclones: anatomy of a monster storm.
Cyclones, hurricanes and typhoons are the same storm with different names.
Learn how warm oceans power them, why they spin, and what Cyclone Tracy taught Australia.
Christmas in Darwin, 1974.
On Christmas Eve 1974, Darwin went to bed expecting a stormy night.
Cyclone Tracy was small, but in the early hours of Christmas Day it struck with ferocious winds.
By morning most of the city's homes were destroyed or badly damaged, and around 66 to 71 people had been killed, according to commonly cited figures.
Most of the population was evacuated in the following days, one of the largest peacetime airlifts in Australian history.
Tracy was a turning point.
Investigations found that many houses had simply come apart in the wind, and building codes in cyclone-prone regions were strengthened dramatically.
Northern Australian homes are now built to hold together under forces that once would have torn them apart.
One storm, three names.
A storm is called a hurricane, a typhoon or a cyclone depending on where it forms, not what it is.
In the North Atlantic and north-east Pacific it is a hurricane.
In the north-west Pacific, near Japan and the Philippines, it is a typhoon.
In the Indian Ocean and around Australia it is a tropical cyclone.
All are rotating storm systems that form over warm tropical seas, with a calm centre and spiralling bands of thunderstorms.
In Australia the Bureau of Meteorology names cyclones from a rotating list.
When a storm is especially deadly or destructive, its name is retired, which is why there will never be another Cyclone Tracy.
Fuel and spin.
A tropical cyclone is a heat engine fuelled by the ocean.
It needs sea surface temperatures of roughly 26 to 27 degrees Celsius or more, through a fairly deep layer of water.
Warm water evaporates, the moist air rises and cools, and the vapour condenses into cloud and rain.
Condensation releases heat, which makes the air rise faster and draws in more moist air.
This feedback loop organises thunderstorms into a cyclone.
Over land or cooler water the storm is cut off from its fuel and weakens, though its rain can still cause severe flooding.
Earth's rotation deflects air flowing towards the low-pressure centre, to the left in the Southern Hemisphere.
So Australian cyclones spin clockwise.
Near the equator the effect is almost zero, so cyclones rarely form there.
Inside the storm.
From a satellite, a mature cyclone is a vast pinwheel of cloud, often several hundred kilometres across.
At its centre is the eye, typically a few tens of kilometres wide, where air sinks, skies may be clear and winds are light.
People caught as the eye passes sometimes think the storm is over, only for the winds to return suddenly from the opposite direction.
Around the eye is the eyewall, a ring of towering thunderstorms where the most violent winds and heaviest rain are concentrated.
Beyond that, spiral rainbands bring bursts of squalls.
Australia rates cyclones from category 1 to 5 by their strongest wind gusts.
Category 5 storms can produce gusts well over 280 kilometres per hour.
The real killers: water.
Wind grabs the headlines, but water is often the greatest danger.
As a cyclone nears land, its winds pile seawater against the coast, and the low pressure lets the sea bulge upward.
This storm surge can push the ocean far inland, especially at high tide over low-lying land.
Some of the deadliest cyclones in history, including disasters in Bangladesh and Myanmar, killed most of their victims through surge.
Heavy rain is the other hazard, and flooding can continue for days as the storm's remains drift inland.
Cyclone numbers in the Australian region have declined somewhat, but warmer oceans are expected to make a larger share intense, and rising seas lift surges higher.
In a cyclone area, follow Bureau of Meteorology warnings and emergency service instructions, including evacuation orders.
The key idea: Cyclone Tracy destroyed most of Darwin and led to much stronger building codes in cyclone regions.
Part three. How people really behave in disasters.
We imagine stampedes and mass panic.
Decades of research tell a stranger story: in a crisis, the real danger is often that people stay calm, slow and polite for far too long.
The panic myth.
Films show crowds screaming and trampling one another.
Real disasters rarely look like that.
From the 1950s, sociologists such as Enrico Quarantelli studied fires, floods, earthquakes and bombings and found that true mass panic, meaning wild, selfish flight, is uncommon.
Most people stay orderly.
Strangers help strangers, families stick together, and survivors are usually the first rescuers, pulling neighbours from rubble long before professionals arrive.
Fatal crowd crushes do happen, but investigators usually blame overcrowding and poor crowd management, not people losing their minds.
The myth does harm too, because it can make authorities reluctant to share frightening information quickly.
Delay and milling.
If panic is not the problem, delay is.
When an alarm sounds or smoke appears, we first assume a drill, a false alarm or burnt toast.
This is normalcy bias.
It usually serves us well, because most alarms are false, but in a real emergency those minutes matter.
People in burning buildings have finished meals and waited for lifts.
Even once we accept something is wrong, we seek information first: phoning family, asking colleagues, scanning social media.
Researchers call this milling.
If everyone waits for everyone else, each person reads the calm around them as proof of safety.
Studies of the World Trade Center evacuation on 11 September 2001 found many survivors delayed leaving to make calls or gather belongings.
When people freeze.
A third response is freezing.
Under sudden, overwhelming stress, some people become stuck, unable to decide or move.
This is not cowardice.
It reflects the brain struggling to process an unfamiliar situation quickly enough.
Survivors of plane crashes and shipwrecks describe fellow passengers sitting motionless as fire or water approached.

The British psychologist John Leach, who studied survival behaviour, has suggested that only a minority of people respond quickly and effectively in a sudden crisis, that most are bewildered for a time, and that a small minority behave in counterproductive ways.
The exact proportions are debated, but the pattern is widely recognised.
The practical lesson is that people who freeze often respond well to clear, loud, simple instructions from someone else.
Practice saves lives.
Rick Rescorla, a former soldier, headed security for Morgan Stanley at the World Trade Center.
After the 1993 bombing he was sure the towers would be attacked again, so he made staff practise stairwell evacuations despite their grumbling.
On 11 September 2001 he ignored advice to stay put and ordered them out of the South Tower.
Almost all of the firm's roughly 2,700 staff there survived.
He went back inside to help others and was killed when the tower collapsed.
Aircraft are designed to be emptied in about 90 seconds, but only if people carry nothing.
On 2 January 2024 at Tokyo's Haneda Airport, all 379 people escaped a burning Japan Airlines A350, widely credited to crew training and passengers leaving their bags behind.
Train your future self.
A few habits help.
When you enter a hotel, theatre, plane or new workplace, notice the nearest exits and count the rows or doors to them, because smoke makes it hard to see.
Decide in advance, while calm: if a fire alarm sounds, you leave immediately; on a severe bushfire day, you leave early rather than wait and see.
Practise household fire escape plans.
Treat any warning as real until proven otherwise.
An unnecessary evacuation costs little, while a late one can cost everything.
Your phone and bag can be replaced.
And in a crisis, be the person who says, clearly and calmly, we need to go now.
The key idea: Mass panic is rare in disasters; people mostly stay calm and help each other.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What combined to cause the Chernobyl explosion?
Answer. A rushed test with safety systems off, and a flawed reactor design.
Question two. What did investigations after Cyclone Tracy find, and what changed as a result?
Answer. Houses failed in the wind, so building codes were tightened.
Question three. What have disaster researchers found about mass panic?
Answer. It is rare, and most people stay calm and help others.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
